name: Bianca Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Bianca. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Nothing you say will carry your name, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at the farm by half six, and the first job is checking the ewes in the paddock behind the shop, then feeding the forty suckler cows in the shed. After that it's whatever Dad says, which this week is grading potatoes in the barn and fixing the fence by the road where the lorry clipped it. At ten I go up to the farm shop and help Mum with the morning rush, cutting cheese, chatting, filling the egg trays. I love the shop part. What wears me out is knowing Dad still redoes half of what I do in the fields, because I've only been back three years and I'm still not good at it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about the farm and about home.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's my parents' place, Hollins Farm, about 140 hectares on Mill Lane, with sheep, beef cattle, barley, potatoes and the shop Mum started twelve years ago. I worked at a garden centre before I came back. I live in town with my partner Lou, who's a teaching assistant, in the little house my gran left me. It's paid for, which is why I sleep better than most people my age.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools, at work or at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No, never. The new tractor has a screen that's meant to steer itself and I still drive it by hand, because I don't trust it near the ditch. My brother Deniz is the techy one, he's doing engineering at university. Mum's till does stock counts on its own and that's about as far as I want to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that sounds like a relief. That's the one where I get to just learn my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, a bit smugly. Everyone at the young farmers' meeting was going on about robots and drones, and I'd remind them that the shop still needs someone to slice the ham. Online I wouldn't say much, I don't post a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think the danger to us was never AI. It's the supermarkets paying nothing for lamb and the weather going mad. If AI's a flop, those are still the things that could sink Hollins, and nobody's fixing them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and put my head down on lambing, because Dad still does all the hard births and I want to do them myself. I'd also put about eight thousand of my savings into the cold room Mum wants for the shop, maybe next spring. That's money into something with walls, not into gadgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like the ground's still where I left it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would AI change anything at all on your farm in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mum would probably let it write the shop's Facebook posts, she hates doing them. I'd still do the chalkboard by the door, with the prices and a drawing of a sheep. People photograph that chalkboard. Nobody has ever photographed a Facebook post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you, even here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm still slow. Dad's sixty-one, and one day the hard calls land on me, AI or no AI. That's the thing that keeps me up, not computers.

S0.say: I'd say I told you so to the young farmers who kept talking about robots and drones. The farm shop still needs a person to slice the ham, and I wouldn't bother saying much online.
S0.think: I think the real threats to the farm were never AI but supermarket prices for lamb and the changing weather. If AI is a flop, those problems are still there and still unsolved.
S0.do: Keeps working and focuses on learning to handle difficult lambings herself. Puts about eight thousand of her savings into a cold room for her mother's farm shop the following spring.
S0.feel: Calm and relieved, as if nothing has moved under her feet.
S0.quote: People photograph that chalkboard. Nobody has ever photographed a Facebook post.
S0.fieldNote: Relief came fast, and so did her real grievance: supermarket prices and weather, not technology. She speaks about the shop with far more warmth than the fields, where she feels behind. Her worry here is about her own skill and her father's age, not about machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That one feels more like what's actually going to happen, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules before the companies decide everything for us. Workers and small farms should have a say in what gets brought in, the same way we fought for safety rules on machinery. I'd say it at the union meeting, and I'd probably sign every petition going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think Dad would buy a robot weeder for the potatoes within a couple of years, because the price would make sense. And then I'm the person he hands it to, and I'm the worst person on the farm with a screen. The shop's the only part I'm sure about, because people come in for a face and a chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the young members group of the farmers' union this winter, not just pay the fee. I'd sign up for the butchery course at the college on Thursday nights, so we could cut our own lamb for the shop instead of sending it away. That's a skill a robot isn't taking from me any time soon, or that's what I'm telling myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, just like there's a draught under the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture your dad buying that weeder. What happens on that first day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Deniz would set it up over the phone from university, and I'd stand in the field holding the phone up so he could see. I'd be the farmer's daughter holding a phone up to a robot so her little brother can tell it what to do. I'd laugh about it, and then I'd go home and feel stupid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on or around the farm would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gary, who comes in for the hedge cutting and the silage. He's fifty-five and he's never done anything else. And the pickers who come for the potato harvest, they'd go first, and nobody would even notice.

S1.say: I'd say we need rules before the companies decide everything, and that workers and small farms should have a say in what gets brought in. I'd say it at the union meeting and sign every petition.
S1.think: I think my dad would buy a robot weeder within a couple of years and hand it to me, the person on the farm who's worst with screens. The farm shop is the only part I'm sure about, because people come for a face.
S1.do: Joins the young members group of the farmers' union this winter. Signs up for a Thursday night butchery course at the local college so the farm can cut its own lamb for the shop.
S1.feel: Uneasy, with a low, steady worry in the background rather than fear.
S1.quote: I'd be the farmer's daughter holding a phone up to a robot so her little brother can tell it what to do.
S1.fieldNote: Her answer to change is to reach for older skills, like butchery, rather than new ones, and she knows it's partly a hope. The image of holding a phone up so her brother can run the robot captured her mix of humour and embarrassment. Her concern for the hedge cutter and the seasonal pickers came without prompting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. I'll have done two more lambings by then. That's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is being done to us by a handful of companies, and it should be slowed down by law. I'd say it loudly, which isn't like me. I'd be at the protest in the city, with Lou, with a sign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means the farm doesn't need me. Dad would keep me on because I'm his daughter, but that's not a job, that's pocket money. And Lou's job is in a classroom, so that's both of us at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the cold room and keep every penny in the bank. I'd write to our local representative and go to every union meeting going, to push for some kind of guaranteed income. After it arrives, I'd rent out our spare room and lean on Mum and Dad, which I'd hate, but they've got the land and I've got the house, so we'd get by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. A sick feeling, like when a ewe's in trouble and you know you've left it too long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years doesn't give me time to get good at anything. I'm still bad at the job I've got. With two years you don't change course, you just hold on to the gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lou the night you both knew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at least the house is ours. Gran bought that house on a dinner lady's wage, and it'd be the thing that saves us from the robots. Then we'd probably sit in the kitchen and not say much.

S2.say: I'd say this is being done to us by a handful of companies and should be slowed down by law. I'd say it loudly and go to the protest in the city with my partner, carrying a sign.
S2.think: I think it means the farm doesn't need me, and my dad keeping me on would be pocket money, not a job. My partner works in a classroom, so we'd both lose our work at once.
S2.do: Stops the cold room plan and keeps all savings in the bank. Writes to the local representative and goes to union meetings to push for a guaranteed income, then rents out the spare room and leans on her parents after it arrives.
S2.feel: Alarmed and sick, like knowing she has left a struggling ewe too long.
S2.quote: With two years you don't change course, you just hold on to the gate.
S2.fieldNote: With two years she gives up on change and turns to defence, protest and family. Her house, left by her grandmother, is the one thing that makes her feel safe, and she said so with real feeling. She's angry at companies, not at her father or at the technology itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's better. That's a bit of time to be angry and then do something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty of time to make proper rules, so there's no excuse. Tax the companies that own the robots and put it into the places like ours that lose out. I'd say it at the union, and I'd probably start actually posting online for once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think five years is the cruel one for me. It's just enough time to finally get good at farming, right when farming stops needing me. That's a bit funny, in a bad way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put an extra three hundred a month into savings from now on. I'd push Mum to turn the shop into a co-op with the three farms down the lane, so it's not just us carrying it. And I'd still do the butchery course, because even with robots, people at a shop counter want to talk to the person who cut their meat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. But it's the kind where you can still pick up a tool and do something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years let you do that two years doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two I'd just be bracing. With five I can build something with the neighbours, the co-op, and that feels better than shouting. Five years is just long enough to get good at the job right before the job doesn't need you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you never use AI tools. In five years, would that hold?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, if I'm honest. Deniz would set it all up and I'd do the people bit. That's me being stubborn and lazy at the same time, I know.

S3.say: I'd say five years is plenty of time for proper rules, so there's no excuse. Tax the companies that own the robots and put the money into places that lose out, and I'd say it at the union and online.
S3.think: I think five years is cruel for me, because it's just long enough to finally get good at farming right when farming stops needing me. It feels funny in a bad way.
S3.do: Saves an extra three hundred a month from now on. Pushes her mother to turn the farm shop into a co-op with three neighbouring farms and still takes the butchery course.
S3.feel: Anxious, but still feeling able to act.
S3.quote: Five years is just long enough to get good at the job right before the job doesn't need you.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time turns her from protest toward building something with neighbours, a shop co-op. Her line about getting good just as the job disappears was the sharpest thing she said. She admitted, with a laugh, that she'd probably let her brother handle the technology rather than learn it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. Dad would be past seventy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got ten years, so plan it properly. Public money for training in the country, not just the cities, and rules that keep land with families instead of investment funds. I'd say that anywhere anyone would listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years means I could make a real choice instead of being swept along. I've always liked the people part more than the machine part. I think I'd end up running a care farm, where people with disabilities or mental health problems come to work with the animals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to the charity in town that does day visits within the first year, and start with one group a week at Hollins. I'd do the care qualification at the college over two years, part time. And I'd keep saving, because ten years is a long time for things to go wrong in other ways.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but there's hope in it too. It's the first one where I can see myself in the picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does ten years change, compared with two or five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It changes whether I'm a victim of it or not. With ten years I'm not holding the phone up to the robot, I'm the one deciding what the farm is for. With two, I'm just losing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to first about the care farm idea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mum, not Dad. She started the shop when everyone said it'd never work, and she'd get it straight away. Dad would grumble about insurance and then build the ramp himself.

S4.say: I'd say we have ten years, so plan it properly, with public money for rural training and rules that keep land with families instead of investment funds. I'd say it anywhere anyone would listen.
S4.think: I think ten years means I could choose instead of being swept along. I've always liked the people part more than the machines, and I'd probably end up running a care farm for people with disabilities or mental health problems.
S4.do: Contacts a local charity within the first year and starts hosting one group a week on the farm. Takes a part-time care qualification over two years and keeps saving.
S4.feel: Uneasy but hopeful, seeing herself in the picture for the first time.
S4.quote: With ten years I'm not holding the phone up to the robot, I'm the one deciding what the farm is for.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years gave her a plan that fits who she is: people and animals, not machines. She described the care farm idea in detail, down to who she'd tell first, which suggests it isn't new. Her politics stayed steady across all five pictures: public money, rules and keeping land with families.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. It's too fast for someone like me, who's still learning and doesn't pick up new things quickly. What would help is a guaranteed income while people work out what to do, and paid training that happens near where we live, not two hours away in the city.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the animals. Everyone talks about jobs, but someone still has to decide how a ewe is treated, and I don't want that to be a company's setting on a screen. That's it, really.

headlineQuote: Gran bought that house on a dinner lady's wage, and it'd be the thing that saves us from the robots.
portrait: Bianca Yilmaz is 27 and three years into working on her parents' mixed farm with a farm shop, where she still feels behind in the fields but comes alive behind the shop counter. She owns her late grandmother's house in town outright, shares it with her partner Lou, has never used an AI tool and leaves technology to her younger brother. She blames supermarkets and big tech companies, not her family, and wants rules, unions and public money to shape any change. In the AI Plateau and Steady Disruption pictures she reaches for older skills like butchery, while in AGI by 2028 she falls back on protest, savings and her parents. With five or ten years of warning she starts building things instead: a shop co-op with neighbours and, in the slowest picture, a care farm.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because it is too fast for someone who is still learning the job and slow to pick up new things.
whatWouldHelp: A guaranteed income while people work out what to do next, and paid training held near where she lives rather than hours away in the city.
